https://artdaily.com/news/199483/How-Art.text: Home Last Week Artists Architects Galleries Museums Photographers Photography PhotoGallery Games Subscribe Comments Search Contact How Art Resists Fascism: Major exhibition to open in Stockholm Kateryna Lysovenko, To be in Vienna seeing people from other wars, 2025. STOCKHOLM .- Bonniers Konsthall is proud to open its landmark autumn exhibition, The Defeated: The Aesthetics of Resistance 2026 (26 August – 8 November 2026). Against a global backdrop of shifting political landscapes, this major international group show explores what resistance to fascism and experimentation with community mean in the contemporary climate of a rising far-right. The exhibition coincides with the lead-up to Sweden’s 13 September general elections, inviting a broader reflection on the role of culture and art in navigating today's complex democratic landscape. The exhibition is deeply rooted in the life and work of the Swedish-German writer and visual artist Peter Weiss (1916–1982). Taking its title from his 1948 post-war reflection The Defeated and his seminal three-volume novel The Aesthetics of Resistance (1975–1981), the exhibition weaves together new contemporary works with historical documents to explore how art can serve as a vital instrument for navigating the complexities of the present. Art as Resistance “If we want to take on art, literature, we have to treat them against the grain, that is, we have to eliminate all the concomitant privileges and project our own demands onto them.” Peter Weiss, The Aesthetics of Resistance Peter Weiss’s three-volume novel The Aesthetics of Resistance (1975–1981) follows a group of young, working-class antifascists in 1930s Europe who use art and literature as intellectual weapons to resist Nazi rule. Weiss argues that reclaiming culture is not a passive luxury but a radical act of resistance, fostering the collective solidarity necessary to envision a world beyond fascism. Bonniers Konsthall’s exhibition brings together a group of artists whose practice resonates with Weiss’s enduring legacy. The exhibition presents new works alongside historical pieces, documents, and artifacts by Peter Weiss (1916, Germany–1982, Sweden), his wife Gunilla Palmstierna-Weiss (1928, Switzerland–2022, Sweden), and their circle, exploring how art can hold space for the 'defeated' and effectively resist dominant forces. Joanna Nordin Asp, Artistic Director of Bonniers Konsthall and co-curator of the exhibition, says: "Our founder, Jeanette Bonnier, urged us to ‘dare to believe in the not yet formulated.’ This has been Bonniers Konsthall’s guiding principle for the past 20 years, and this exhibition at this time in history epitomises that call to action more than any other.” “Against a backdrop of war, historical disorientation, and fractured public spheres, cultural institutions are an important frontline in the conflict over democracy, justice, and national identity. In this context, Peter Weiss’s The Aesthetics of Resistance emerges not as a static historical novel, but as a vital instrument for navigating the complexities of the present and the future. With this exhibition, we invite you to explore how art can illuminate these struggles and help us envision new possibilities for the future.” Curatorial Concept & Highlights “And now we became truly aware of this architecture of contradictions, which was overloaded and bare, fragmentary but with perfected details, which sought its way from the hard to the soft, from the rough to the smooth, which emerged from ancient times and hinted at things to come.” Peter Weiss, The Aesthetics of Resistance Curated as a 'waking dream,' the exhibition mirrors Weiss's literary technique and his transition from the surrealist 'dream of sleep' found in The Defeated to the active political engagement of The Aesthetics of Resistance. Eschewing linear chronology, the show utilises a spatial montage to place historical artifacts alongside new works by contemporary international artists who engage with Weiss's legacy through direct address or thematic resonance. The Defeated: The Aesthetics of Resistance 2026 is curated by Kim West, François Piron, and Joanna Nordin Asp, and is a cornerstone of Bonniers Konsthall’s 20th anniversary programme. Kim West, co-curator of the exhibition, says: "We want visitors to navigate the exhibition autonomously, making edits that uncover connections - even those unintended or unforeseen. The space is designed as a 'place of associations,' where boundaries are removed to allow for constant interplay. Through the deliberate use of transparencies, screens, and bleeding audio, we dissolve the divide between individual works, fostering a unified environment where every element is in conversation with the next." In a contemporary world marked by the resurgence of the far-right and new forms of fascism, what does an 'aesthetics of resistance' mean today? Participating artists Hamedine Kane & Valérie Osouf (b. 1983, Senegalese-Mauritanian; lives in Dakar and Brussels; b. 1972, France; lives in Paris): Present Where the Seams Hold Against the Fixed Narrative (2026) as part of the School of Mutants collective. The work is a large textile assemblage configured like a boat sail that evokes Géricault's painting Raft of the Medusa. It utilizes a documentary editing technique, sewing together images of historical and recent liberation movements, Pan-Africanism, and portraits of heroes to revive internationalist networks. Chiara Bugatti (b. 1991, Italy; lives in Stockholm): Explores memory, power, and permanence through sculpture and installation. Her installation Poses and Postures (2026) draws on her grandfather's silent drawing sessions and past as an Italian partisan/Nazi prisoner, fusing his drawings with cast stone sculptures made from leftover marble and granite—materials heavily tied to fascist architecture and power. Ali Cherri (b. 1976, Lebanon; lives in Paris): Presents The Summoner (Grafting) (2026), a hybrid sculpture combining an Italian stone fountain head with a headless Thai statuette torso to challenge canonical representations of power. His slideshow, A Monument to Subtle Rot (2024), pairs images of toppled statues with a poetic essay by Palestinian writer Karim Kattan regarding collective memory and undetermined belonging. Zbyněk Baladrán (b. 1973, Czech Republic; lives in Prague): In Oracles / Protocols (2023–2025), the artist uses geomancy to repeatedly ask when and where the next bombing of the Gaza strip will happen. By utilising an ancient irrational system to address the conflict in Gaza, he forces a confrontation with the irrational when ethical systems fail. The work features abstract reliefs, scribbled representations of ruined Palestinian landscapes, and diagrams of international companies supplying weapons to Israel. Öyvind Fahlström (1928–1976, Brazilian-Swedish; lived in Sweden and USA): Focuses on historical ties with Peter Weiss, who filmed Fahlström's abstract explosion drawings in 1961. Fahlström evolved in the late 1960s from surrealism toward critical, figurative history paintings and diagrammatic world models/maps of the 1970s that confronted global capitalism and imperialism. Harun Farocki (1944, Czechia–2014, Germany): Highlights Farocki's connection to Weiss, including a recorded 1979 German television interview focused on The Aesthetics of Resistance, where Weiss stated his fiction was built entirely on a realistic, uninvented basis. Farocki’s own documentary films utilize deep archive research to critique media and commit to historical and political struggles. Jean-Luc Godard (1930, France–2022, Switzerland): Features a short film festival trailer that serves as a dazzling poem and tribute to the closing lines of Weiss's novel, summarizing a shared persistence of hope despite failed struggles. Like Weiss, Godard used documentary montage to throw "blocks of past into the present" to rupture dominant historical narratives. Ane Hjort Guttu (b. 1971, Norway; lives in Oslo): Contributes the multi-screen installation On the Ground (2026), which plays with the concept of horizontality. One screen shows non-taking-off planes at Schiphol airport overlaid with a monologue describing dreams as horizontal and vulnerable, but fascism as vertical. Other screens show historical Dutch landscape paintings of the same airport area and bouncing Suprematist elements. Kateryna Lysovenko (b. 1989, Ukraine; lives in Vienna): Features the painting Madness of Fascism (2026), which explores the asymmetrical relationship between victim and perpetrator during war. It depicts a fascist family in front of a theatrical backdrop of human organs, questioning systemic violence, ideology, and whether perpetrators act with conscious direction or total indifference. Asier Mendizabal (b. 1973, Spain; lives in Bilbao and Stockholm): Presents Hiru's covers I (La estética de la resistencia) (2026), a tribute to Eva Forest, the anti-Franco activist who founded the Hiru publishing house and printed the Spanish translation of Weiss's novel. The work consists of coarse fabric draped over wood to mimic an open book, utilizing Hiru’s signature diagonal graphic line to evoke the history of collective book-reading groups. Peter Nestler (b. 1937, Germany; lives in Sweden): Showcases his 10-minute film Sightseeing (1968), which juxtaposes scenic, peaceful summer images of Stockholm with a narrated German text detailing the devastating US napalm bombings in North Vietnam. The stark montage underscores how Western prosperity is paid for by destruction elsewhere, while occasionally drawing dreamlike, unexpected visual correspondences between the two landscapes. Daniela Ortiz (b. 1985, Peru; lives in Cuzco): Looks to popular and agitprop puppet theater for her Swedish-translated audio play, Luka and the Magic Beans (2025), which critiques agro-industries that exploit the working class while using fascism to scapegoat immigrants. She also showcases painted sculptures detailing the history of the German weapons manufacturer Krupp and its collaboration with the Nazi regime. Gunilla Palmstierna-Weiss (1928, Switzerland–2022, Sweden): Summarizes her eight-decade career as a core collaborator and co-creator of many of Peter Weiss's works. The section outlines her extensive archival research for stage sets and costumes—such as the metal junk "Bogey" sculpture from 1966—alongside her deep anti-colonial commitments in Cuba and Vietnam, and her work shaping Sweden’s New Cultural Policy. Christoffer Paues (b. 1975, Sweden; lives in Stockholm): Features Sketches for Six Antifascist Flags (2026), a mixed-media assemblage of large banners responding to the six parts of Weiss's novel by integrating historical icons (Pergamon frieze fragments, Spanish republican stars, ship propellers) with quotes from artists like Sonia Delaunay. It includes four videos showing streams of images and a public performance around Stockholm. Samuel Richter (b. 1993, Sweden; lives in Berlin and Norrköping): Documents the film Die Reise des Reichskommissars... (2026), which weaves together two parallel late-19th-century German colonial efforts: the excavation and transport of the Pergamon Altar to Berlin, and Ernst Heinrich Göring’s negotiations in Namibia that led to the century's first genocide. The film cross-references historical diaries and paintings to critique how classical European imagery was used to justify brutal colonial empires. Lenke Rothman (1929, Hungary–2008, Sweden): Focuses on the Swedish-Hungarian artist's habit of stitching everyday debris into artwork. As a Holocaust survivor, her featured piece The Family (1984) commemorates her original family lost to concentration camps, while a separate portrait series on folded bedsheets depicts historical role models like the murdered socialist leader Rosa Luxemburg. Lina Selander (b. 1973, Sweden; lives in Stockholm): Focuses on the multi-channel film installation Binding the Dream (2026), created with Oscar Mangione, which investigates how art can remain politically useful by mastering its own media and form. The piece blends archival leftovers from Peter and Gunilla Weiss with imagery of sculptural models from Swedish sculptor Carl Eldh, focusing on a concrete, historical concept of resistance. Beyond the Gallery Walls The Defeated: The Aesthetics of Resistance 2026 is a centerpiece of Bonniers Konsthall’s 20th-anniversary year, extending its reach through a series of collaborative projects. These include a public education course developed with the Institute for Advanced Studies of Political Aesthetics (IAS), which has hosted a year-long evening programme exploring The Aesthetics of Resistance. The project also features an international academic conference, The Theater of Divided Worlds: Peter Weiss’s The Aesthetics of Resistance and the Challenge of Critical Universality in the Twenty-First Century, organised by the Institute for Research on Migration, Ethnicity and Society (REMESO) at Linköping University, taking place 29–30 October 2026, with Thursday’s sessions hosted at Bonniers Konsthall. Rounding out the initiative is an ambitious forthcoming book featuring, alongside Peter Weiss’s writings, newly commissioned essays by leading intellectuals and curators, including Magnus Bergh, Claudia Firth, Anna Hallberg, Esther Leslie, Sven Lütticken, Joanna Nordin, François Piron, Jacques Rancière, Werner Schmidt, Gustav Strandberg, Alberto Toscano, and Kim West. https://www.nrc.nl/nieuws/2026/08/30/eur.text: Terug naar de krant „THE WORLD is a healthier but not a safer place,” wrote The Economist in 1953 after the death of Joseph Stalin. One of the bloodiest tyrants in history had just dropped dead and this newspaper fretted over who and what might come next. It was not alone in its apprehension. Well-known Russian totalitarianism seemed somehow more manageable than whatever the future held. Fast-forward seven decades and the sentiment has changed little. No matter what the Kremlin does, fears that, if resisted, it may do something even more reckless are still used as an argument for caving in to Russian demands. De redactie van NRC selecteert de beste artikelen uit The Economist voor een breder perspectief op internationale politiek en economie. Take a conversation with Andrey Melnichenko, a Russian oligarch, published recently in these pages. He acknowledged that Vladimir Putin had made mistakes but argued that whatever comes next could be worse still; that Russia, if pushed too hard, might „descend into chaos, brutal autarky or a sullen, dangerous dependency”, or even „use a tactical nuclear weapon”. The bottom line was clear: let Russia do as it pleases, or else. It is a dead-end approach. For years after the fall of the Soviet Union, the West bent over backwards not to humiliate Russia and to turn it into a responsible international stakeholder. In 1997 alone Moscow was invited to join the G7, signed the NATO–Russia Founding Act and entered into a Partnership and Co-operation Agreement with the European Union. Since the fall of the Soviet Union, each American presidential administration has tried to bring Russia into the fold by signing treaties, looking its leader deep in the eyes or pressing reset buttons. So did former Soviet satellite states, including Poland. In 2009 Mr Putin was invited to attend ceremonies at Westerplatte in Poland to commemorate the 70th anniversary of the outbreak of the second world war. My country introduced a visa-waiver programme for Russians living close to our border in the Kaliningrad exclave. The heads of the Russian Orthodox and Polish Roman Catholic churches issued a joint appeal, calling for „forgiveness of wrongs, injustice and every evil committed against each other”. I am still personally vilified by our opposition for saying that I could imagine a genuinely democratic Russia joining NATO, once it met all the criteria. We all tried. And we were all turned down. Today, almost five years after igniting the bloodiest European war since 1945, Russia is again trying to get its way by threatening escalation. Only recently it warned Britain of „consequences” for providing Ukraine with military assistance. The visit of John Ratcliffe, the CIA’s director, to Moscow this month was allegedly an attempt to warn the Kremlin against assaulting a NATO member state. And yet, while the Russian leader displays no willingness to reach any peace deal—save Ukraine’s capitulation—still too many refuse to acknowledge the reality. Some argue that Russia has become so weak under mounting economic and military pressure that the West should negotiate before the regime collapses, or worse, before the state fragments and produces even more dangerous successors to Mr Putin. Others insist that Russia should not be pushed too far because it might resort to further escalation, including in the nuclear domain. Both arguments are misguided. Fears that sustained pressure would result in the state’s break-up are overstated. Russia’s highly centralised political system has made its regions economically, administratively and financially dependent on Moscow. Millions of citizens rely on transfers from the federal budget, and even resource-rich regions depend on centrally controlled transport and energy infrastructure. Russia is not the Soviet Union. Outside the North Caucasus, ethnic Russians remain an overwhelming majority, and the memory of economic crisis and political chaos that accompanied the Soviet Union’s dissolution continues to dampen separatist sentiments. Last but not least, the country has been heavily centralised for centuries. Major political changes have historically originated in Moscow, not in the regions. Even in the event of a leadership crisis, or a grave military setback, the more likely consequence would be a struggle within the ruling elite to control the centre, not a dissolution. Threats of escalation—issued either by the authorities or suggested by allegedly concerned oligarchs—are not reactions to new crises but part of a long-established playbook. Today, as in the past, Russia is testing the West by force. Soviet military doctrine called this tactic razvedka boyem, „reconnaissance by combat”. Limited attacks were used to expose opponents’ positions, strengths and weaknesses before launching a larger offensive. The Kremlin has applied the same principle ever since. In its current fight against Western democracies, it deploys drones, cyber-attacks, sabotage, GPS interference and information warfare. These are not random provocations. They are carefully calibrated tests of resolve. The question is no longer whether Russia is probing NATO. It is whether NATO understands that it is being probed, and what signal it intends to send to prevent grey-zone actions from turning into full-fledged confrontation. The Kremlin operates on a simple assumption: not that Russia is stronger, but that democratic adversaries will hesitate to test its vulnerabilities. Europe should therefore resist the temptation to engage in premature negotiations. Those calling to reopen political dialogue may hope that discussions will eventually reduce tension. In the long run the opposite is true. Dialogue begun before Russia’s strategic position has weakened sufficiently may strengthen the Kremlin’s domestic legitimacy, encourage further hybrid operations, undermine European support for Ukraine and deepen divisions within our democratic community. The uncomfortable truth is that Europe must accept greater risk in the short term to avoid far more serious dangers in the future. Our objective cannot be merely to avoid escalation. It is to convince Mr Putin and his people that escalation will get them nowhere, and that we are willing to sacrifice more than money to stand up for ourselves. We have what it takes. European leaders’ primary responsibility is to protect their people from Russian threats, not to protect Russia from itself. Russia regards us as the enemy and wants to destroy our democratic civilisation. We should not rush to appease it. When Mr Putin is ready for peace he will find a way to communicate it. Radek Sikorski is Poland’s foreign minister and deputy prime minister. © 2026 The Economist Newspaper Limited. All rights reserved. https://shipandbunker.com/news/world/391.text: Subscribe Get Daily Email Contact Us Sign in Home News & Features Compliance Costs Bunker Prices Bunker Intelligence World News Latest Features World Americas EMEA Asia/Pacific Home News & Features World Diplomacy-Hungry Traders Cause Oil To Drop, Despite Ongoing Iran-Houthi Hostilities Diplomacy-Hungry Traders Cause Oil To Drop, Despite Ongoing Iran-Houthi Hostilities Iran threatened with new weapons while the Houthis bragged about more Saudi attacks on Saudi Arabia: File Image/Pixabay The increasingly familiar and arguably naïve hope among investors that a return to diplomatic progress between the U.S. and Iran would prevail this week caused oil prices on Monday to drop by over 4 percent – even though both sides continued issuing threats on Sunday. The optimism derived from the impending visit to the United Nations of Iranian president Masoud Pezeshkian , and U.S. president Donald Trump stating he would be open to meeting him. Bob Yawger , director of energy futures at Mizuho , said, "Just a couple days ago that would have seemed like ⁠a very far-flung idea; it's a move in the right direction." It's a move in the right direction As a result, Brent settled down $3.53 , or 3.4 percent , at $100.34 per barrel; West Texas Intermediate settled down $4.52 , or 4.5 percent , to $95.78 per barrel. Also affecting trading on Monday was Saudi Aramco , which loaded about 14 million barrels of crude on seven supertankers inside the Mideast Gulf ‌on Sunday; satellite data showed that Saudi oil transiting the Strait of Hormuz averaged 2.9 million barrels per day (bpd) over the past six days, up from just 700,000 bpd in August. Another development widely perceived as promising was China , which according to Iranian sources asked the Islamic republic to help curtail the Houthis at the request of Riyadh . Still, it’s unclear if the optimism will last long enough for oil prices to fall much further: the Houthis claimed to have attacked Riyadh as well as a Saudi ‌Aramco facility in the Red Sea city of Yanbu with cruise and ballistic missiles plus drones; as for diplomacy with Iran, on Monday its leaders warned https://www.foxnews.com/live-news/iran-war-donald-trump-strait-of-hormuz-09-21 that it would deploy new weapons and expand the geography of the conflict if the U.S. launches another offensive. For his part, Trump told media he was still weighing three options: “Wipe it out, let it rot with the economy, or make a deal." In other oil news on Monday, output at the Sharara field, Libya ’s largest oil field, was cut by more than half after an armed group shut a pipeline running to the Zawiya export terminal; the field is capable of pumping about 127,000 bpd. Also on Monday, Hungary under the new leadership of prime minister Peter Magyar asked Washington not to levy tariffs on the central European country, which still buys oil from Russia. Marton Hajdu , chair of the Foreign Policy Committee in Hungary’s parliament, said in a Facebook post that he also asked U.S. lawmakers of both sides of the aisle to “help Hungary reduce its reliance on Russian energy and ensure its energy supply from multiple sources.” Hungary is one of the biggest importers of Russian crude oil, following China, India , and Turkey . https://www.politico.eu/article/center-r.text: BRUSSELS — A rebellion by center-right lawmakers has exposed deep divisions over a flagship EU industry bill, threatening to derail negotiations over how far Europe should go to protect its manufacturers from foreign competition. The attempt by three European People’s Party lawmakers to torpedo the Industrial Accelerator Act quickly gained support last week within European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s political family. The challenge is unlikely to attract enough support to kill the legislation outright. But it lays bare rifts over the bill’s central “Made in Europe” provisions that threaten to paralyze negotiations in the European Parliament and among EU governments, raising the prospect of indefinite delays or a compromise that waters down the bill beyond recognition. Advertisement Advertisement The proposal, championed by Industry Commissioner Stéphane Séjourné, would steer public procurement and subsidies toward European manufacturers in sectors including renewable energy, steel and automobiles. But it has sparked clashes over which countries should qualify for preferential treatment. Séjourné challenged the critics on Friday, accusing them of undermining the very industrial strategy they have demanded from Brussels. “I would just say please be coherent,” he told reporters. “You can’t ask for a text to be scrapped and then at the same time say that it’s not moving fast enough.” The German-Swedish trio from the center-right EPP — Christian Ehler, Angelika Niebler and Jörgen Warborn — submitted their amendment to reject the Commission’s Industrial Accelerator Act proposal last Tuesday. Another 20 EPP lawmakers, the largest group in the Parliament, signed on . They warned that a restrictive interpretation of Made in Europe risks plunging the bloc into “multiple trade wars with some of our closest partners.” The Parliament’s draft report “would unilaterally break many of the EU’s free trade agreements and WTO obligations, which opens our flank for retaliation,” they wrote. In or out The backlash has exposed a deeper split within the EPP over how far the EU should go in favoring European manufacturers — and raises questions about whether the lawmakers steering the IAA through Parliament can assemble a majority for their preferred approach. While only a minority of the EPP’s 184 lawmakers signed the rejection amendment, more than half the group support a broader definition of Made in Europe that would initially include most of the EU’s trading partners, according to a Parliament official briefed on the negotiations. Advertisement Advertisement That puts them at odds with the three lawmakers leading the Parliament’s work on the bill. The lead lawmakers — Renew’s Christophe Grudler, socialist Pierre Jouvet and Green Anna Cavazzini — argue that extending preferential treatment too far would undermine the purpose of the legislation. “It would no longer be ‘Made in the EU,’ no longer ‘Made with the EU,’ but ‘Made Everywhere,’” Grudler told a recent joint committee hearing. The rejection amendment was meant as a “political signal” and did not intend to kill the IAA outright, according to four people familiar with the EPP’s thinking. The rebels had wanted to drive home their opposition to restricting Made in Europe to the EU’s 27 members, while leaving open the possibility of a broader compromise. “Bold moves are necessary, because the citizens and the industry expect results. We go ahead with our proposals and let’s see if a majority is possible to be formed around them,” said Romanian MEP Lóránt Vincze, one of the co-signatories. Without commenting publicly on the rebellion, EPP leader Manfred Weber has given national delegations room to take their own positions on the IAA. At a group meeting in Strasbourg last week, Weber described the bill as a “complex” file and said delegations could propose amendments reflecting their preferences, according to internal notes seen by POLITICO. Advertisement Advertisement “The group has not endorsed this amendment, and it will probably take its position once there is a clear compromise in the Council,” an EPP official said. The divisions leave the three lead lawmakers with an uncertain path to a majority in the Parliament, particularly if the EPP coalesces around a broader definition of Made in Europe than the one they are proposing. Divided governments The dispute goes beyond the European Parliament. EU governments are also struggling to agree on how narrowly to define Made in Europe, with France pushing to reserve preferential treatment for a relatively small group of countries while Germany and other more free-trade-oriented governments want to extend it to a broader range of trading partners. The central disagreement is between a restrictive “opt-in” approach, under which trading partners would have to qualify for preferential treatment, and a broader “opt-out” model that would initially include more countries but then allow the EU to exclude those that fail to meet certain conditions. France wants a narrow club, and has won the support of Italy, Greece and Cyprus, according to readouts of a recent meeting of deputy ambassadors in Brussels. Germany and 13 other member countries prefer a broader “Made with Europe” club that would include most trading partners. Eligibility would depend on reciprocity, including whether partners offer European companies comparable access to their public procurement markets. The distinction matters beyond the EU’s borders. While China is a principal target of the proposed measures, a restrictive interpretation of Made in Europe could disadvantage close partners such as the U.K., which is lobbying for favorable treatment ahead of a November summit on resetting relations with the EU. Advertisement Advertisement Among the options under discussion, Spain has proposed a three-tiered system for trading partners to qualify for Made in Europe, while Poland and at least 12 other countries have concerns about the methodology for defining low-carbon requirements, which they argue could disadvantage some member states. Narrow path MEPs have submitted some 5,300 amendments to the draft report authored by Grudler, Jouvet and Cavazzini. These reveal competing models: partner access with safeguards, a tightly defined European preference, or investment allowed only with substantial local commitments. The sheer number of amendments underscores the challenge of finding a workable compromise on a proposal already branded “a bureaucratic monster” by the Federation of German Industries, a leading industry lobby. The Irish EU Council presidency wants to deliver a new compromise text as soon as this week and finalize the general approach of member states in late November. With EU countries still divided, it’s unclear whether it can meet that deadline — unless a potential grand bargain under discussion between France and Germany materializes. The Parliament faces its own difficult timetable, with lawmakers struggling to reconcile the thousands of amendments. The EPP remains divided over the scope of Made in Europe, while support for the narrower approach of the lead lawmakers is far from assured even within their own political groups. If the regulation’s geographical scope ends up being too broad, “almost any country around the world can become a hub for repackaging Chinese equipment, changing a few nuts and bolts and then selling it in the European market as made in the EU,” warned Sander Tordoir, chief economist at the Centre for European Reform. Yet the disagreements may be less fundamental than they appear, according to Tristan Beucler of Strategic Perspectives, a pan-European think tank. Beucler pointed to emerging accord among EU governments on issues such as reciprocity and preventing circumvention, while noting that the rejection amendment does not represent an agreed EPP position. “The IAA’s objectives are widely shared in the European Parliament and Council,” Beucler said.
